People think we write everything down because we are formal. That is not the reason. We write everything down because half the team is in another country and will read it eight hours later, when nobody can ask a question. So the rules are simple. The minutes go out within twenty-four hours, with one owner and one date for every action item. That one is flexible, if somebody is travelling. The rule I never negotiate is the decision log. Every decision goes in, with a date and a name. Not the discussion, just the decision. Six months later, when somebody asks why the base plate changed, the log answers in ten seconds instead of ten emails. And one more thing, which is only advice: if an email needs more than five lines, you should call instead. Long emails in a second language are where projects go quiet.

The most expensive thing on my last project was not a mistake. It was silence. We asked the other office a question about a foundation load, and nobody answered. Our engineer asked again, politely, and waited. Then he waited some more. By the time it reached me, nine days had gone, and the concrete was already scheduled. Now, when I explain this to a new engineer, I tell them the truth about why they waited. They think escalating means complaining about a colleague. It does not. In a project with three time zones, escalating just means the question is bigger than the two of you. So the rule in my team is two days. Two days with no answer, you escalate, and you copy the person you are escalating about, so nothing happens behind anybody's back.

This briefing is about action items, because most of ours are badly written. A good action item has four things, and only four. A verb, so we know what happens. An owner, one single name. A date. And a place where the result will appear: a drawing, a log, an email to a distribution list. If one of the four is missing, the item will still be open in November. The most common problem is the owner. If the owner is the team, nobody is the owner. Write the name. The second most common problem is the item that nobody has started after two calls. That is not a task, it is a wish. Either give it a real owner and a real date, or delete it from the minutes and say why you deleted it. An honest list of six is worth more than a polite list of twenty.
